human_tolerance.notes: Roosts by day hanging from foliage in trees, including in settled areas, and is often found where insects concentrate around street lighting. Wikipedia records deaths from flying into cars, tall human-made structures and wind turbines, and it is attacked by hawks, owls, blue jays and crows.

phases.name: mating
phases.note: The breeding season starts in the autumn, and multiple males can sire a single litter.

phases.name: absent
phases.note: In winter the species occurs in the southeastern United States and northeastern Mexico with greatest concentrations in coastal areas, and in spring and summer it can be found in the Great Lakes and Great Plains regions; Michigan stands in here for the Great Lakes part of that statement, which is the northern limit of the summer range.

phases.name: young
phases.note: Pups are born in the summer, usually sometime between May and July. A female has four nipples, which allows her to nourish multiple offspring at once. Pups learn to fly about a month after being born, after which they are weaned; even then they remain with the mother a while before roosting on their own.

conservation.note: Wikipedia's Conservation section states it meets the criteria for least concern because of its wide range, large population size, occurrence in protected areas, tolerance of some habitat disturbance, and a population unlikely to be declining rapidly.

range.note: Widely distributed in eastern North America and Bermuda, generally east of the Continental Divide including southern Canada and northeastern Mexico. In winter it occurs in the southeastern United States and northeastern Mexico with greatest concentrations in coastal areas; in spring and summer the Great Lakes and Great Plains regions. Former western, Central American and northern South American populations have been reassigned to the desert red bat.

traits.limb_count.note: Authored judgement: a bat is a four-limbed mammal whose forelimbs are modified as wings, matching the schema's walking-limb count of 4.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: Its wings are long and pointed, and their aspect ratio and wing loading indicate that eastern red bats fly relatively quickly and are moderately maneuverable; it climbs to roost by hanging from branches.

traits.nest_type.note: None is the mapping: the species is shown hanging from a branch and roosting in a tree, and builds no nest of any of the schema's kinds.

traits.perching.note: Set to true for the roosting behaviour: the article's photographs and text describe a red bat hanging from a branch and a female roosting in a tree, and pups stay with the mother hanging from a cloth.

traits.mass_kg.note: Midpoint of Wikipedia's 7-13 g weight range.

traits.length_m.note: Wikipedia's stated 109 mm from head to tail.

traits.wingspan_m.note: Honest gap: Wikipedia gives no wingspan for this species. 0.10 m is authored judgement, bounded by what the article does give: the stated 109 mm head-to-tail length is a floor, and the stated 40.6 mm forearm is a little under 40 percent of it, which is the proportion a wing of this genus spans. No open source used here gives a wingspan.

traits.lifespan_y.note: 'Allen Kurta argues that the lifespan for an eastern red bat is about two years, although they can probably live even longer.'

traits.diet.note: 'Eastern red bats are insectivorous, preying heavily on moths, with other insect taxa also consumed', including named pest moths such as gypsy, tent caterpillar, cutworm and coneworm moths. With no plant component recorded, invertebrate is the whole diet.

traits.social.note: Honest gap: the article describes no group behaviour beyond females remaining with their pups and multiple males siring one litter, so Solitary is the judgement mapping and the upper bound of 2 covers a mother with a single pup.

traits.activity_pattern.note: Derived, and stated as such: Wikipedia does not use the word nocturnal for this species. It describes the bat hanging from a branch and roosting in a tree, preying heavily on moths, which are night-flying insects, in a family (Vespertilionidae) whose members forage at night, and it records the bats being active in flight rather than hunting from a perch. Nocturnal is the judgement that follows from that.

traits.defense.note: The species is attacked and killed by hawks and owls and by blue jays and crows, and the hawk is described as a major predator of bats hiding in leaf piles; escape is by flight, so Flee is the judgement mapping.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement: a fast, wary flier that is recorded as killed in numbers by cars, tall structures and wind turbines, and that hangs motionless in daylight where it is easily disturbed.

habitat.use.note: The strong aerial share follows the wing description and the fast, maneuverable flight it implies, together with a mostly night-going life; the arboreal share covers hanging from foliage to roost, and the small ground share covers the leaf piles and ground roosts mentioned as a hawk's hunting ground. The three shares are authored judgement.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Authored judgement from the described roosting: the bat hangs from a branch, so a perch is the nearest available tag.

habitat.resources.note: The single invertebrate resource follows traits.diet exactly; the perch entry covers the hanging roost and the perch weight is judgement.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Wikipedia records tree roosting illustrated by photographs of a bat hanging from a branch and a female roosting in a tree, and records deaths from flying into cars, tall human-made structures and wind turbines, and predation by hawks, owls, blue jays and crows. The note about insects concentrating at street lighting is not stated in the article and is left out; the tree-roosting and collision records are what carry the entry.

seasonal.strategy.note: Migration is the mapping of the article's statement that in winter the species occurs in the southeastern United States and northeastern Mexico with greatest concentrations in coastal areas, and in spring and summer in the Great Lakes and Great Plains regions, with males and females sharing the same range throughout the year. No overwintering site is described, so no dormancy phase is claimed.

seasonal.phases.note: The autumn start of the breeding season, the summer birth window of May to July, the four nipples, and the month to flight and weaning of pups are all from Wikipedia's Reproduction and life expectancy section.

seasonal.life_stages.note: The duration follows Wikipedia's statement that pups learn to fly about a month after being born and then stay with the mother a while before roosting alone; the scale is authored judgement.

vocalizations.note: Deliberately empty. A bat's navigation is by echolocation, which is not one of the schema's vocalisation contexts, and Wikipedia's biology and reproduction sections as used here describe no social call, so none is invented.

look.note: Colours from Wikipedia: males are brick or rusty red and females a slightly more frosted shade of red, and the whole body is densely furred including the uropatagium, with back hairs about 5.8 mm and uropatagium hairs 2.6 mm long. The uropatagium and ruff parts render the tail membrane and the frosted female shading the description names, with the ruff kept small so that it reads as a collar rather than covering the head, and the large ear_ratio renders the ears characteristic of the genus name Lasiurus, 'hairy tail'. The biped_winged mesh is the only winged plan available and is built for birds, so its beak stands in for the bat's muzzle; that compromise is recorded here.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared ground-forager program, using it as a generic forage-flee-rest machine for a flying nocturnal animal rather than as a ground feeder. Both gaits are 'fly' because the animal forages and flees in the air; the sun band is left at the program's daytime default so the bat roosts by day and forages at night; food_tag is 'invertebrate' from the moth diet. All radii are judgement, on the pattern of the ground foragers in this repository.
